passages.happening:
Jesus appoints “seventy-two others and sent them two by two ahead of Him to every town and place He was about to visit” (verse 1). “The harvest is plentiful,” he tells them, “but the workers are few” (verse 2). They are to pray for more workers.

He sends them out “like lambs among wolves” (verse 3). They are to carry no purse, no bag, no sandals, and not to stop and greet people on the road. In a house, they are to say, ‘Peace to this house.’ They are to stay in one house, eat what they are given, heal the sick, and say, ‘The kingdom of God is near you.’

Where a town will not welcome them, they are to wipe its dust off their feet in the street, and still say, ‘The kingdom of God is near.’ It will be more bearable for Sodom on that day than for that town.
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells of this second sending. The twelve were sent in chapter 9. Now a larger group goes ahead of Jesus on the road to Jerusalem, two by two, like scouts preparing a welcome.

Seventy, or seventy-two? Bibles differ. The King James Version says seventy; the BSB and many modern Bibles say seventy-two. The early copies of Luke are divided, and scholars still argue about which number Luke wrote. Both numbers had meaning for Jewish hearers. Genesis 10 lists the nations of the world descended from Noah's sons: seventy of them in the Hebrew text, seventy-two in the old Greek translation. If that is in the background, the number points to the whole world that will one day hear the message. Moses also chose seventy elders to share his work, and two more, Eldad and Medad, received the Spirit in the camp (Numbers 11:16, 26).

The rules are like the ones for the twelve: travel light, accept hospitality, do not shop around for a better house. ‘Do not greet anyone along the road’ is not a rule against being polite. The point is urgency: nothing on the way is to hold them up.

‘The worker is worthy of his wages’ (verse 7) became a rule in the early church. Paul quotes the same words when he says that those who teach should be supported (1 Timothy 5:18).
passages.ot:
The ‘Lord of the harvest’ is God. The prophets used the harvest as a picture of the time when God gathers his people. Isaiah sees God gathering Israel one by one, like grain beaten from the stalks (Isaiah 27:12).

Sodom was the city the Old Testament remembered as the worst of all (Genesis 18:20). To say it will be better off than a town that refused God's messengers is a shocking way of saying how much was being offered.
passages.hard: Is wiping off the dust a curse, or a sign of contempt for people who say no? No. It is a public sign that the messengers have done their part, and that the responsibility now lies with the town. Notice that even then they are to say, ‘The kingdom of God is near.’ The last word to a town that refused them is still the good news. Nothing here allows anyone to harm or punish those who turn the message down. Jesus had just rebuked two disciples for wanting exactly that (9:54-55).
passages.asks: Jesus told them to pray for workers before he sent them as workers. Prayer and going belong together. Ask who you are praying for. And notice the first word they were to say on entering a house: ‘Peace’. What would it mean for you to bring peace first into the homes you enter?

passages.t: Woe to the towns that had seen the most
passages.happening:
“Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!” (verse 13). If the miracles done in them had been done in Tyre and Sidon, those cities would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. And Capernaum, will it be lifted up to heaven? No, it will be brought down to Hades.

Then Jesus says to the seventy-two, “Whoever listens to you listens to Me; whoever rejects you rejects Me; and whoever rejects Me rejects the One who sent Me” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Matthew gives these woes in another place (Matthew 11:20-24), and the note there explains them. ‘Woe’ is a prophet's cry, closer to ‘alas’ than to a curse: grief and warning mixed together. Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum were near neighbours on the north side of the Sea of Galilee. They had seen the most.

Tyre and Sidon were Gentile cities on the coast to the north, outside Israel. Sackcloth was rough cloth worn in mourning, and ashes were put on the head as a sign of sorrow. Jesus says that pagan cities would have taken his works more seriously than the towns where he had lived.

Luke puts these words in the middle of the sending. The messengers need to know what is at stake, and that they do not go in their own name. To listen to them is to listen to Jesus.
passages.ot: The prophets spoke against Tyre's pride. Ezekiel tells its ruler, “Your heart is proud, and you have said, ‘I am a god’” (Ezekiel 28:2). The words about Capernaum echo Isaiah's taunt over a proud king who said, “I will ascend to the heavens”, and was told, “But you will be brought down to Sheol, to the lowest depths of the Pit” (Isaiah 14:13, 15). Hades is the Greek word for Sheol, the place of the dead.
passages.hard: Does God judge places, not people? The towns stand for their people. Jesus' point is not about buildings but about what people did with what they saw. He also says it will be ‘more bearable’ for some than for others. Many readers take that to mean that judgment is fair and measured: those who were shown more are answerable for more. Jesus will say the same in 12:48.
passages.asks: The towns that saw the most were not the ones that turned. It is possible to grow up close to the things of God and never take them seriously. Ask what you have seen and heard of Jesus, and what you have done with it.

passages.happening:
The seventy-two come back full of joy. “Lord, even the demons submit to us in Your name” (verse 17).

Jesus answers, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (verse 18). He has given them authority to tread on snakes and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy. Nothing will harm them. “Nevertheless, do not rejoice that the spirits submit to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke has these words. The disciples' joy is real, and Jesus does not scold it. But he moves it to a better place.

What did Jesus mean by Satan's fall? Readers have taken it in three main ways. Some think Jesus is describing what he saw while the seventy-two were out: as they drove out evil spirits in his name, the enemy's power was being broken. Some think he is speaking of Satan's fall long before, when he first rebelled against God. Others hear a prophecy of the defeat to come at the cross and resurrection. Many hold the first, with the others in the background. All agree on the main point: in Jesus' work, evil is losing.

Lightning falls fast, and from high up. The picture is sudden and complete.

Snakes and scorpions were real dangers in that dry country. Here they also stand for ‘all the power of the enemy’. The promise is protection in the work Jesus gives, not a guarantee that nothing hard will ever happen. Luke's own second book tells of Stephen killed (Acts 7:59-60) and of James put to death (Acts 12:2).
passages.ot:
Isaiah mocked the fallen king of Babylon: “How you have fallen from heaven, O day star, son of the dawn!” (Isaiah 14:12). Many Christians later applied those words to Satan. A psalm promises the one who trusts God, “You will tread on the lion and cobra; you will trample the young lion and serpent” (Psalm 91:13).

Names written in heaven echo the book of life. Moses prayed to be blotted out of “the book that You have written” (Exodus 32:32), and Daniel was told that at the end “everyone whose name is found written in the book” will be delivered (Daniel 12:1).
passages.hard:
Is the promise about snakes meant literally? This is not an invitation to test God by handling real snakes or walking into danger on purpose. When the devil quoted Psalm 91 to Jesus and told him to throw himself down from the temple, Jesus refused: “Do not put the Lord your God to the test” (4:12). The promise is that the enemy cannot finally harm those who belong to God.

And why not rejoice in power over spirits? Because power can be lost, misused, or envied, and because it is not what saves anyone. What lasts is belonging to God. A person with no gift anyone can see has exactly the same reason for joy as the most gifted.
passages.asks: The disciples were thrilled by what they could do. Jesus pointed them to what had been done for them. Ask where your joy comes from: from your results, or from being known by God. If you feel you have done little that anyone would notice, hear this: your name written in heaven is the best news, and it is just as true for you.

passages.happening:
“At that time Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit” (verse 21). He prays aloud, praising the Father, “because You have hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children” (verse 21). All things have been handed to him by his Father. No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.

Then he turns to the disciples privately: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see” (verse 23). Many prophets and kings longed to see and hear what they are seeing and hearing, and did not.
passages.hearers:
Matthew has this prayer too (Matthew 11:25-27), and the note there explains it. ‘The wise and learned’ would make hearers think of the experts in the Law. ‘Little children’ points to fishermen, tax collectors and ordinary people. It is not praise of ignorance. It is about how a gift is received: a small child does not earn what a parent gives.

Only Luke says Jesus ‘rejoiced in the Holy Spirit’. The word is strong: he was full of joy. This is one of the few places in the Gospels where we are told Jesus was glad. And Luke shows all three, Father, Son and Spirit, in a single verse: the Son rejoices in the Spirit and praises the Father.

The last words look back over the whole Old Testament. Prophets and kings had hoped for the day God would keep his promises. The disciples are living in it.
passages.ot: Kings and prophets did long for this. Isaiah looked for a day when “the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped” (Isaiah 35:5). Peter later wrote that the prophets “searched and investigated carefully” the salvation that was to come (1 Peter 1:10).
passages.hard: Does God hide the truth from clever people on purpose? The point is not that God is against learning. Luke himself was an educated writer who checked his sources (1:1-4). The point is that pride shuts the eyes. People who think they already know are often the last to receive. Anyone, clever or simple, can become a ‘little child’ who receives.
passages.asks: Jesus was glad that ordinary people understood. Do you think of faith as something you must be clever enough to master? It is a gift to receive. And notice what Jesus called blessed: not having power, but seeing. Ask what you have been given to see that others longed for.

passages.happening:
An expert in the law stands up to test Jesus. “Teacher,” he asks, “what must I do to inherit eternal life?” (verse 25).

“What is written in the Law?” Jesus replies. “How do you read it?” (verse 26). The man answers with two commands: love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, strength and mind, and love your neighbour as yourself. “You have answered correctly,” Jesus says. “Do this and you will live” (verse 28).

“But wanting to justify himself, he asked Jesus, ‘And who is my neighbor?’” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
An ‘expert in the law’ was a scholar of the Law of Moses, someone whose work was to explain and apply it. ‘To test’ need not mean he was hostile. Teachers tested one another with hard questions; it was how debate worked. But Luke hints at his motive: he wanted to justify himself, to show that he was in the right.

In Mark and Matthew, it is Jesus who names the two great commandments, in a different setting (Mark 12:28-34; Matthew 22:34-40). Here the lawyer names them himself, and Jesus agrees. The two commands are not new. Joining them was the heart of the matter, and Jesus tells him he has it right.

Then comes the real question. If I must love my neighbour, where does ‘neighbour’ stop? Who is inside the circle, and who is outside it? The lawyer wants a line.
passages.ot:
The two commands come straight from the Law. “And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength” (Deuteronomy 6:5). “Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against any of your people, but love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18).

The same chapter of Leviticus already pushes the line out: “You must treat the foreigner living among you as native-born and love him as yourself” (Leviticus 19:34). The Law itself would not let ‘neighbour’ mean only ‘people like me’.
passages.hard: ‘Do this and you will live.’ Is Jesus teaching that we earn eternal life by keeping the commandments? He is answering the lawyer on his own ground, from the Law, and the Law does promise life to those who keep it (Leviticus 18:5). But no one loves God with all their heart and their neighbour as themselves without fail. The lawyer's next question shows he already knows it, and is looking for a smaller command he can manage. The rest of Luke shows where that leads: to mercy for those who know they have not kept it (18:13-14).
passages.asks: The lawyer asked a good question and then tried to shrink the answer. Ask whether there is a command of God you have quietly made smaller, so that it fits what you are already doing. ‘Who is my neighbour?’ is often a way of asking, ‘Who can I leave out?’

passages.happening:
Jesus tells a story. A man is going down from Jerusalem to Jericho. Robbers attack him, strip him, beat him, and leave him half dead.

A priest happens to be going down the same road. When he sees the man, he passes by on the other side. A Levite does the same.

“But when a Samaritan on a journey came upon him, he looked at him and had compassion” (verse 33). He goes to him and bandages his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He puts him on his own animal, brings him to an inn and cares for him. The next day he gives the innkeeper two denarii and says, ‘Take care of him, and on my return I will repay you for any additional expense.’

“Which of these three do you think was a neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of robbers?” Jesus asks (verse 36). “The one who showed him mercy,” the lawyer replies. “Go and do likewise,” Jesus says (verse 37).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this story, and it is probably the best known Jesus ever told.

The road. Jerusalem stands high in the hills; Jericho lies far below, near the Jordan. The road between them ran about twenty-five kilometres and dropped about a thousand metres, through dry, rocky, empty country. That is why the man was ‘going down’. Joshua names a pass on that road, the Ascent of Adummim (Joshua 15:7). Adummim means ‘red’, probably from the colour of the rocks. The Christian scholar Jerome, writing around AD 400, said the place was called that because of the blood shed there by robbers. Whatever the name meant, the road's lonely stretches made a robbery easy to believe.

The priest and the Levite. Priests served at the altar in the temple. Levites were from the tribe of Levi and helped in the temple's work. They were the most religious people a hearer could name. Why did they pass by? Many sermons say they were afraid of becoming unclean. A priest was not to make himself unclean for a dead person, except for close family (Leviticus 21:1-3), and the man looked half dead. But that explanation is debated. Both men were going down the road, away from Jerusalem, so they were not hurrying to serve in the temple. The Law gave Levites no such rule about the dead. And a later Jewish teaching, written down in the Mishnah around AD 200, says that even a high priest must become unclean to bury a body that no one else will bury (Mishnah Nazir 7:1). How far that later teaching shows what people thought in Jesus' day is not known. The scholar Richard Bauckham argued (New Testament Studies, 1998) that the story sets two duties against each other, keeping clean and loving your neighbour, and shows that love must come first. Jesus himself gives no reason at all. Whatever their reasons, the story gives them no excuse.

The Samaritan. The note on John 4 explains who the Samaritans were. They worshipped the God of Israel and kept the five books of Moses, but at their own mountain, Gerizim. Jews and Samaritans had a long history of bad feeling and violence on both sides. Many readers think a Jewish hearer would expect the third man in the story to be an ordinary Jewish layman, the hero after the two officials. Instead Jesus makes the hero a Samaritan. Just a chapter ago, a Samaritan village refused to welcome Jesus (9:53). Samaritans are not only people in an old story. A small Samaritan community, about nine hundred people, still lives today.

The care. Olive oil was a common medicine, and wine, many think, was used to clean the wounds. He walks while the wounded man rides. Two denarii was two days' pay for a labourer (Matthew 20:2). And he promises to come back and pay whatever more it costs. That is a blank cheque, given to a stranger's innkeeper, for a man he had never met.
passages.ot:
There is an old story like this in the Bible, and many readers think Jesus had it in mind. When the northern kingdom, whose capital was Samaria, captured people from Judah, a prophet told them to let the captives go. Men from Samaria “provided from the plunder clothing for the naked. They clothed them, gave them sandals and food and drink, anointed their wounds, and put all the feeble on donkeys. So they brought them to Jericho, the City of Palms, to their brothers” (2 Chronicles 28:15). Clothing, oil on wounds, donkeys, the road to Jericho: and the helpers came from Samaria.

The prophets had long said that God wants mercy more than ritual: “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6).
passages.hard:
Jesus turns the lawyer's question around. The lawyer asked, ‘Who is my neighbour?’, meaning ‘Whom must I love?’ Jesus asks, ‘Who was a neighbour?’, meaning ‘Who acted as one?’ The question is no longer where the line is drawn around me. It is whether I will be a neighbour to whoever is lying in front of me. And notice that the lawyer cannot bring himself to say ‘the Samaritan’. He says, ‘The one who showed him mercy.’

The story has been read in more than one way. Some early Christian teachers, Augustine among them, read it as a picture of salvation: the wounded man is Adam, fallen humanity; the Samaritan is Christ, who comes to the rescue; the inn is the church. Many readers today think that reading misses Jesus' own point, which ends with ‘Go and do likewise.’ Others say both can be true: we can do what the Samaritan did only because Christ did it first for us.

The story is not the programme of a political party, of the left or the right. It is not only a call to be nice either. It asks for mercy that costs time, money and safety, given across a line of old hatred, to anyone in need. That is hard, and it should not be softened.
passages.asks: The question is not ‘Who is my neighbour?’ but ‘Whose neighbour am I willing to be?’ Ask who you have been passing by on the other side, with good reasons ready. And ask who in your world is ‘the Samaritan’: the person you were raised to look down on. Jesus made that person the one who did right. ‘Go and do likewise.’

passages.happening:
As they travel on, Jesus comes to a village where a woman named Martha welcomes him into her home. Her sister Mary “sat at the Lord’s feet listening to His message” (verse 39).

Martha is distracted by all the work of getting a meal ready. She comes to Jesus and says, “Lord, do You not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her to help me!” (verse 40).

“Martha, Martha,” the Lord replies, “you are worried and upset about many things. But only one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, and it will not be taken away from her” (verses 41-42).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this story. Luke does not name the village. John tells us that Martha and Mary lived in Bethany, near Jerusalem, with their brother Lazarus, and that Jesus loved all three (John 11:1, 5).

To ‘sit at the feet’ of a teacher meant to be his student. Paul says he was “educated at the feet of Gamaliel” (Acts 22:3). A saying kept in the Mishnah, written down around AD 200, tells people to let their homes be a meeting place for the wise and to sit in the dust of their feet (Mishnah Avot 1:4). So Mary is not simply resting. She has taken the place of a disciple, and Jesus defends her right to be there. Many scholars think it was not the usual place for a woman in that world, and Jesus says it will not be taken from her.

Martha is doing what a good host was expected to do. Welcoming a guest, and his followers, meant a great deal of work: water to draw, bread to bake, food to cook. She is the one who opened her home in the first place.

Notice how Jesus answers her. He says her name twice, gently. He does not say her work is bad. He names what is wrong with her heart: she is ‘worried and upset about many things’.
passages.ot: Moses told Israel that “man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 8:3), and Jesus quoted it when he was hungry in the desert (4:4). Mary has chosen that word. A psalm says it simply: “Be still and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10).
passages.hard:
Is this story a ranking: prayer above work, quiet people above busy ones? It is often read that way, but Luke does not set it up so. Just before this, Jesus told the lawyer to ‘go and do’ like the Samaritan. Luke has already praised the women who served Jesus from their own means (8:3), and Jesus will say that he himself is “among you as one who serves” (22:27). Doing and listening both belong to following him. The trouble was not that Martha served. It was that she served anxious and resentful, and wanted Jesus to take her sister away from his feet.

Nor is this a story about which work belongs to women. If anything, it opens a door: a woman sits where disciples sit, and Jesus says that place is hers.

If you are the Martha, the one who keeps everything running while others seem free to rest, Jesus is not scolding you. He sees how much you carry, and he says your name with love. He is inviting you to sit down too. The work will still be there. And the ‘one thing’ is offered to you as freely as to Mary.
passages.asks: Martha was serving Jesus and missing him at the same time. Ask whether that is you: busy for God, and too busy to listen to him. What would it look like to sit at his feet for a while this week, with the work left undone? And if you are a Mary, ask who is carrying the load so that you can sit, and how you might share it.
